claims.text: Pt nanoparticles around 3.5 nm provide superior ethanol-oxidation activity compared with approximately 2 nm and 5 nm particles.
Pt nanoparticles around 3.5 nm provide superior selectivity in ethanol oxidation compared with approximately 2 nm and 5 nm particles.
Pt nanoparticles around 3.5 nm provide superior durability in ethanol oxidation compared with approximately 2 nm and 5 nm particles.
Nanoparticle size governs the proportion of exposed crystal facets on the Pt surface.
Nanoparticle size governs the proportion of undercoordinated sites on the Pt surface.
Reducing Pt nanoparticle size increases the fraction of undercoordinated surface sites.
Changes in the fraction of undercoordinated Pt sites alter the adsorption energies of ethanol.
Changes in the fraction of undercoordinated Pt sites alter the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
At approximately 3.5 nm, the balance of Pt surface sites facilitates the complete 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
At approximately 3.5 nm, the balance of Pt surface sites suppresses the accumulation of poisoning species.
Approximately 2 nm Pt particles may be less stable because they over-expose undercoordinated sites.
Approximately 2 nm Pt particles may promote excessive side reactions because they over-expose undercoordinated sites.
Approximately 5 nm Pt particles may provide too few active interfaces for optimal ethanol oxidation.
The approximately 3.5 nm catalyst will exhibit the highest catalytic current density among the tested particle sizes.
The approximately 3.5 nm catalyst will show greater selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation than the approximately 2 nm and 5 nm catalysts.
The approximately 3.5 nm catalyst will retain current better over time than the approximately 2 nm and 5 nm catalysts.
The proposed particle-size dependence applies to ethanol oxidation in 0.1 M KOH at ambient temperature.
The proposed particle-size relationship may fail at substantially different pH values or temperatures, or for other substrates where support effects or different mechanisms dominate.
